about: Time-sensitive factual claims in the catalogues. status 'compiled' = written from general knowledge, never checked against a source (due immediately); 'verified' = checked against the listed sources on 'checked' (due again after review_interval_days). See MAINTAINING.md.

claims.claim: Recorded Future, a threat-intelligence platform, was acquired by Mastercard: the deal was announced 12 Sept 2024 and finalized/closed 20 Dec 2024.
Flashpoint acquired social-media/OSINT vendor Echosec Systems, announced 3–4 Aug 2022.

Microsoft Defender Threat Intelligence (Defender TI) was built on Microsoft's acquisition of RiskIQ, announced 12 July 2021 and closed 18 Aug 2021. As of 1 Aug 2026 Microsoft retired the standalone Defender TI portal/product and folded its data and Intel Explorer experience into ‘Threat intelligence in Microsoft Defender’, serving Defender XDR and Microsoft Sentinel — there is no longer a standalone ‘Microsoft Defender Threat Intelligence’ product as of today (7 Oct 2026).

claims.claim: VirusTotal has been owned by Google since its 2012 acquisition (announced 7 Sept 2012); it now operates under Google Cloud as part of the ‘Google Threat Intelligence’ offering, still free for the public web tier.
DomainTools acquired Farsight Security (maker of DNSDB passive DNS) on 9 Nov 2021 and continues to sell DNSDB under the Farsight brand.

Orbis is owned by Moody's, which acquired Bureau van Dijk (completed 2017, ~$3.3B deal); World-Check is owned by LSEG (London Stock Exchange Group), which acquired Refinitiv (World-Check's then-owner) in an all-share deal that completed 29 Jan 2021.

Meta's CrowdTangle, the free public-insights tool widely used by journalists and researchers to track Facebook/Instagram content, was shut down on 14 August 2024. Meta's replacement, the application-based Meta Content Library (and Content Library API), now covers Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp Channels but is restricted to vetted academic researchers and nonprofits and, per contemporaneous reporting, reproduces only a fraction of CrowdTangle's features.

X (Twitter) ended broad free API access starting 1–2 February 2023 and rolled out paid tiers (Basic at $100/month) beginning 8–29 February 2023, eliminating free-tier access for most third-party developers and researchers. Reddit announced on 18 April 2023 that it would begin charging for API access; the new commercial pricing took effect 1 July 2023 and drove third-party apps such as Apollo to shut down.
ADS-B Exchange was acquired by JETNET, a leading aviation-data provider, announced 25 Jan 2023; adsb.lol and airplanes.live grew afterward as community-run, unfiltered alternatives.

Clearview AI has been fined by at least four European data-protection authorities: Italy's Garante (€20M, final decision 10 Feb 2022), France's CNIL (€20M, 17 Oct 2022, plus a further €5.2M non-compliance penalty imposed in 2023), Greece's Hellenic DPA (€20M, final decision 13 July 2022) and the Netherlands' Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens (€30.5M, decision 16 May 2024 / announced 3 Sept 2024).

Maxar Technologies was taken private by Advent International/BCI in May 2023 and split into Maxar Intelligence (earth-imagery) and Maxar Space Systems (hardware) later that year. On 1 Oct 2025 the Maxar name was retired entirely: Maxar Intelligence now trades as Vantor and Maxar Space Systems as Lanteris Space Systems. 'Maxar' is therefore a legacy/historical brand, not the current one.
claims.note: Corrected on verification; catalogue text updated.

claims.claim: SpiderFoot (smicallef/spiderfoot on GitHub), the open-source OSINT automation tool, currently ships 'over 200 modules' per its own README, consistent with the catalogue's '200+ modules' figure.
ICANN made RDAP (not WHOIS) the mandatory gTLD registration-data lookup protocol, with the WHOIS sunset taking effect on 28 January 2025 for ICANN-contracted gTLD registries/registrars.

The EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689), in force since 1 Aug 2024, Art. 5(1)(e) prohibits placing on the market, putting into service or using AI systems that create or expand facial-recognition databases through untargeted scraping of facial images from the internet or CCTV footage — a provision aimed at Clearview AI-style collection.

DSA (Regulation (EU) 2022/2065) Art. 40 lets vetted researchers request access to very large online platforms'/search engines' internal data to study systemic risks; the Commission adopted the implementing delegated act specifying vetting and access procedures on 2 July 2025, which entered a 3-month Parliament/Council scrutiny period before taking effect, with the first vetted researchers expected from around October 2025.

ODNI and CIA jointly released the IC OSINT Strategy 2024-2026 on 8 March 2024 (ODNI News Release No. 06-24), and ODNI separately published its Commercially Available Information (CAI) Policy Framework in May 2024.

The four standard reference cases for US scraping/CFAA law are: Van Buren v. United States, 593 U.S. 374 (2021) (Supreme Court adopts the narrow 'gates-up-or-down' reading of 'exceeds authorized access,' rejecting purpose-based CFAA liability); hiQ Labs, Inc. v. LinkedIn Corp., 938 F.3d 985 (9th Cir. 2019), reaffirmed 31 F.4th 1180 (9th Cir. 2022) on remand (scraping logged-out public pages does not violate the CFAA even after a cease-and-desist, because no technical access barrier was bypassed) — though hiQ separately lost on a breach-of-contract theory in the district court in November 2022 and the parties settled via consent judgment in December 2022, after which hiQ ceased operating; Meta Platforms, Inc. v. Bright Data Ltd., No. 3:23-cv-00077-EMC (N.D. Cal. 23 Jan 2024) (summary judgment largely for Bright Data on Meta's contract claims over logged-out scraping); and X Corp. v. Bright Data Ltd., No. 3:23-cv-03698-WHA (N.D. Cal.) (9 May 2024 order dismissed X's first amended complaint, citing hiQ's public-interest-in-data-access language and Copyright Act preemption of the scraping/reselling claims; a second amended complaint reviving several access-based claims — trespass to chattels, contract breach, CFAA — was allowed to proceed in a 26 Nov 2024 order; the case ultimately settled and was closed 1 July 2025 without a final merits ruling).

In Meta Platforms, Inc. v. Bright Data Ltd. (N.D. Cal., Judge Edward Chen, order filed 23 Jan 2024), the court granted summary judgment largely in Bright Data's favor on Meta's contract claims over scraping logged-out public Facebook/Instagram pages. In X Corp. v. Bright Data Ltd. (N.D. Cal., Judge William Alsup, order filed 9 May 2024), the court dismissed X's first amended complaint's claims over scraping logged-out public data (citing Copyright Act preemption and hiQ's public-interest reasoning); Bright Data did not, however, win final judgment in the X case — X amended its complaint, several access-based claims (trespass to chattels, contract breach, CFAA) were allowed to proceed in November 2024, and the parties ultimately settled, with the case closed 1 July 2025.
Zyte (formerly Scrapinghub, rebranded Feb 2021) is the company behind Scrapy; Zyte's own site states its engineers maintain Scrapy and that fixes land upstream before reaching Zyte's own products.

On 25 November 2022 (decision publicly announced 28 November 2022) the Irish Data Protection Commission fined Meta Platforms Ireland €265 million over a 2019-discovered dataset of scraped Facebook user phone numbers and other personal data exposed via a since-fixed contact-import/'Find Friends' API vulnerability, finding violations of GDPR's data-protection-by-design-and-default requirement (Article 25).

On 19 May 2022 the US Department of Justice issued a revised CFAA charging policy stating prosecutors should not bring charges against individuals 'engaged in good-faith security research' and acting consistent with 'good practice,' where their conduct is 'designed to avoid any harm to individuals or the public, and where the information derived from the activity is used primarily to promote the security or safety of the class of devices, machines, or online services.'

The Robots Exclusion Protocol (robots.txt) was formally standardized by the IETF as RFC 9309 in September 2022. In the OWASP API Security Top 10 2023 edition (released 3 July 2023 via blog, finalized with the 0x11 ranking page), Broken Object Level Authorization (API1:2023) is ranked first.

Since Android 7.0 (Nougat, API level 24), apps no longer trust user-installed CA certificates by default under the Network Security Configuration; developers must explicitly opt in (e.g. via <trust-anchors> with <certificates src="user"/>) to trust them.

App Store binaries are protected with Apple's FairPlay DRM: the Mach-O executable is encrypted and only decrypted at runtime on genuine hardware with Apple's keys, so extracting readable code requires dumping the decrypted binary from memory on a jailbroken device (this remains true as of 2026; FairPlay has not been removed or replaced for App Store distribution).

Play Integrity API and Apple App Attest are the current device-attestation APIs as of 2026; Google's older SafetyNet Attestation API was deprecated starting 2022 and was fully shut down in January 2025, with Play Integrity as its mandated successor.
Telethon's GitHub repository was archived in 2026.

X API: free tier ended Feb 2023, paid Basic/Pro/Enterprise tiers introduced (Basic $100/mo); further restructured since into pay-per-usage credit pricing. Reddit: announced paid commercial API terms 18 Apr 2023, effective 1 Jul 2023, prompting third-party app shutdowns (e.g. Apollo, June 2023). CrowdTangle: shut down 14 Aug 2024, succeeded by the access-gated Meta Content Library. Dataminr: as of 2026 still holds its long-standing commercial data-reseller partnership giving it full X/Twitter firehose access for its real-time alerting products (Dataminr maintains an active 'X' integration/marketplace page and has disclosed the arrangement in litigation and press as recently as March 2024).

Meta Platforms, Inc. v. Bright Data Ltd. (N.D. Cal., Judge Edward Chen, 23 Jan 2024): summary judgment granted largely in Bright Data's favor on Meta's breach-of-contract claims over scraping logged-out public Facebook/Instagram pages, because Bright Data never agreed to Meta's terms by accessing public pages without an account. X Corp. v. Bright Data Ltd. (N.D. Cal., Judge William Alsup): a 9 May 2024 order dismissed X's first amended complaint — access-based claims (trespass, contract, fraud) for failure to allege unauthorized access/damage, and scraping/reselling claims as preempted by the Copyright Act — citing hiQ's concern that letting platforms gatekeep public data risks 'information monopolies.' This was not X's final loss: in a 26 Nov 2024 order the court granted X leave to amend and revived its trespass-to-chattels, Section 17200 (unlawful/fraudulent prong), tortious-interference and contract-breach claims (now alleging concrete server-impairment damages and deceptive scraping conduct), while still rejecting the 'unfair business practices' theory and the copyright-preempted scraping/reselling claims. The parties then settled; the case was stayed in June 2025 and formally closed 1 July 2025 with no final merits judgment. hiQ Labs, Inc. v. LinkedIn Corp.: 9th Cir. affirmed a preliminary injunction for hiQ in 2019 (938 F.3d 985); the Supreme Court vacated and remanded in light of Van Buren (14 June 2021); the 9th Circuit reaffirmed its CFAA holding on remand (31 F.4th 1180, 18 Apr 2022); but in November 2022 the N.D. Cal. district court ruled hiQ had separately breached LinkedIn's User Agreement, and the parties reached a consent-judgment settlement in December 2022 — hiQ, which had been financially struggling throughout, ceased operating after the case closed.

claims.claim: PACER charges $0.10 per page for documents, docket sheets and search results, capped at $3.00 (30 pages) per document; fees are waived for any quarter in which a user accrues $30 or less. Effective 1 Jan 2027 a temporary five-year increase raises the rate to $0.12/page and the automatic waiver threshold to $40/quarter — the first PACER fee change since 2012.

US ocean bills of lading filed with CBP's Automated Manifest System are public records, but 19 CFR 103.31(d) lets an importer/consignee (inward manifests) or shipper (outward manifests) file a certification with CBP's Vessel Manifest Program Manager requesting that its name, address and identifying marks be withheld from public disclosure and from the AMS bulk CD-ROM/data feed; each certification is valid two years and renewable. Commercial redistributors (e.g. S&P Global/Panjiva, ImportGenius, Descartes Datamyne) license the resulting AMS feed, which necessarily excludes any records for which confidentiality was granted.

Companies House's current free bulk-data product is the Free Company Data Product: a snapshot of basic data for all live companies on the register, delivered as ZIP files of CSV data (either one large file or split into 7 parts), refreshed monthly — compiled through the end of the previous month and republished within 5 working days of month-end (the file live on download.companieshouse.gov.uk as of 7 Oct 2026 is dated 2026-10-01). Companies House separately publishes a Free Accounts Data Product (daily/monthly ZIP files of filed company-accounts documents) and a PSC data product.

RDAP became ICANN's mandated gTLD registration-data protocol on 28 January 2025, replacing WHOIS; separately, ICANN's Centralized Zone Data Service (CZDS) grants approved applicants no-cost access to participating gTLD zone files under a standard per-registry Terms and Conditions agreement (restricting marketing use, redistribution and query volume), with ccTLD zone/bulk-WHOIS access negotiated and often paid separately per national registry.
DomainTools announced its acquisition of Farsight Security, the passive-DNS/DNSDB vendor, on 9 Nov 2021.

JARM, an active TLS server fingerprinting tool, was released and open-sourced by Salesforce's engineering team in November 2020 (preceded by Salesforce's 2017 passive JA3/JA3S fingerprinting work); the salesforce/jarm GitHub repository remains live and unarchived as of 2026 (1,300+ stars, open issue tracker), i.e. not formally deprecated, though it has seen no major feature development since release.

CAIDA's UCSD Network Telescope was historically a routed-but-unused IPv4 /8 block; as of 2026 CAIDA's own catalogue describes it as a globally routed but lightly utilized /9 and /10 network prefix under CAIDA stewardship, not a full /8.
claims.note: Corrected on verification; catalogue text updated.

claims.claim: Microsoft's Digital Crimes Unit (DCU) has repeatedly pursued US civil court orders to seize/sinkhole botnet C2 domains in coordination with industry partners, including the March 2020 Necurs takedown (with BitSight and other partners, after ~3 years of research) and the October 2020 Trickbot disruption (court order from the US District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia); Shadowserver Foundation is a nonprofit that independently runs sinkholes and shares victim/infection telemetry with national CERTs/ISPs at no charge; abuse.ch (now part of a Swiss nonprofit ecosystem) operates sinkhole-adjacent feeds (ThreatFox, URLhaus).
Spire Global, Inc. (NYSE: SPIR) completed its acquisition of exactEarth Ltd. on 30 Nov 2021 (deal announced 14 Sept 2021), gaining exactEarth's satellite-AIS business, ~$18M ARR and 150+ customers.

NOAA's final rule amending 15 CFR Part 960, published 20 May 2020 (85 FR 30790), replaced the prior case-by-case shutter-control review for commercial remote-sensing (Earth-observation) satellite licenses under the Land Remote Sensing Policy Act of 1992 with a tiered, risk-based review, while preserving government authority to impose temporary operating restrictions during security-sensitive events; it remains the current version of Part 960.

ADS-B Exchange was acquired by JETNET (announced 25 Jan 2023); community-run alternatives such as adsb.lol and airplanes.live grew afterwards, keeping the no-filtering policy ADS-B Exchange was known for.

Facebook, Inc. (renamed Meta Platforms in Oct 2021) announced its acquisition of Mapillary, the Swedish crowd-sourced street-level imagery startup, on 18 June 2020. The acquirer at the time of the deal was Facebook, not Meta — Meta is the company's current name, acquired under its prior name.
claims.note: Corrected on verification; catalogue text updated.

claims.claim: Hiya's own App Data Protection and Privacy Policy (effective 2018, last reviewed 1 Mar 2024) discloses that it processes 'if a number is stored in your contacts (only if you grant us access to contacts)' and that it matches 'information in user phone logs and contacts with numbers from the calls the user makes or receives ... with information in our database' — i.e. contact-book-based collection for its caller-ID/spam database is directly and publicly documented by Hiya itself, not merely inferred.
claims.note: Corrected on verification; catalogue text updated.

claims.claim: FTC location-data-broker orders under FTC Act Section 5, in chronological order: (1) X-Mode/Outlogic — complaint announced 9 Jan 2024, order finalized 12 Apr 2024, banning sale/sharing of any sensitive location data, requiring deletion of historical sensitive data and a supplier-consent-verification program (first order to flatly ban a data category). (2) InMarket Media — complaint announced 18 Jan 2024, order finalized 1 May 2024, banning sale/sharing/licensing of any precise location data and requiring deletion and a consent-withdrawal mechanism. (3) Avast/Jumpshot — complaint and proposed order announced 22 Feb 2024, finalized 27 Jun 2024, requiring Avast to pay $16.5M and banning sale/licensing of web-browsing data for advertising; Jumpshot itself was shut down in Jan 2020. (4) Gravy Analytics/Venntel — proposed order announced 3 Dec 2024, finalized 14 Jan 2025, banning sale/use/disclosure of sensitive location data (including sales to government agencies via Venntel); Gravy also separately disclosed a data breach exposing location records. (5) Mobilewalla — proposed order announced 3 Dec 2024, finalized mid/late Jan 2025, banning collection of data via RTB exchanges beyond ad-auction purposes and sale of sensitive location/demographic data. (6) Kochava — sued by the FTC in the District of Idaho in Aug 2022 (amended 2023, second amended 2024); this was litigated, not settled, for nearly four years until a stipulated final order was proposed 4 May 2026 and entered by the court 26 Jun 2026, banning Kochava and subsidiary Collective Data Solutions from selling/sharing sensitive location data without affirmative express consumer consent for 10 years, with required sensitive-location-list maintenance, supplier-consent auditing and consumer deletion rights.
claims.note: Corrected on verification; catalogue text updated.

claims.claim: On 29 Apr 2024 the FCC issued forfeiture orders fining AT&T ~$57.3M, Verizon ~$47M, T-Mobile $80M and Sprint tens of millions more (T-Mobile/Sprint combined ~$92M) — nearly $200M total — for selling real-time subscriber location data to data aggregators that resold it onward, including to bounty hunters/a Missouri sheriff via the Securus service, without verifying consent at each hop. The carriers paid under protest and challenged the orders in different circuits on Seventh Amendment jury-trial grounds: the 5th Circuit vacated AT&T's order (2025); the 2nd Circuit denied Verizon's petition; the DC Circuit unanimously upheld the Sprint/T-Mobile forfeitures (15 Aug 2025). The Supreme Court resolved the circuit split in FCC v. AT&T / Verizon Communications v. FCC, decided 4 Jun 2026: it held FCC forfeiture orders under 47 U.S.C. §503(b)(4) do not violate the Seventh Amendment because they don't themselves compel payment and carry no weight in the mandatory jury trial de novo needed to actually collect, reversing the 5th Circuit (reinstating AT&T's fine) and affirming the 2nd Circuit (Verizon's fine stands); Verizon's rehearing request was denied in Aug 2026, making the fines final.
claims.note: Corrected on verification; catalogue text updated.

claims.claim: GM's OnStar Smart Driver feature collected drivers' precise geolocation and driving-behaviour data (sometimes as often as every 3 seconds) via a misleading enrollment flow and, without adequate consumer notice/consent, sold it to data brokers including LexisNexis Risk Solutions and Verisk, where it fed insurance pricing; GM ended the Smart Driver programme and those broker relationships in 2024. The FTC announced a complaint and proposed consent order on 16 Jan 2025 (5-year ban on sharing geolocation/driver-behaviour data with consumer reporting agencies), and finalized a 20-year order on 14 Jan 2026 (2-0 Commission vote) that bars GM/OnStar from disclosing consumers' geolocation and driver-behaviour data to consumer reporting agencies for five years and, for the full 20-year term, requires affirmative express consent before collecting/using/sharing connected-vehicle data, a consumer right to request a copy of or delete their data, an ability to disable precise-geolocation collection where technically possible, and an opt-out of geolocation/driver-behaviour collection.
claims.note: Corrected on verification; catalogue text updated.

claims.claim: Mastercard announced its acquisition of Recorded Future on 12 Sept 2024 and closed it 20 Dec 2024; Equifax announced its acquisition of fraud-prevention vendor Kount on 8 Jan 2021 and closed it 10 Feb 2021 for $640M; Google completed its $5.4B acquisition of Mandiant on 12 Sept 2022 and in May 2024 launched the ‘Google Threat Intelligence’ brand combining Mandiant with VirusTotal data.
claims.note: Corrected on verification; catalogue text updated.

claims.claim: PADFA, enacted 24 Apr 2024 as Division I of H.R. 815, took effect 23 June 2024 (60 days after enactment), banning data brokers from selling or licensing Americans' sensitive personal data to foreign-adversary countries/entities. Separately, DOJ's Executive-Order-14117-implementing final rule (28 CFR Part 202), published in the Federal Register 8 Jan 2025, became effective 8 Apr 2025, with certain audit, reporting and due-diligence compliance obligations phased in to 6 Oct 2025.

California's Delete Act (SB 362, 2023) directed the CPPA to build the DROP deletion portal. The CPPA adopted DROP regulations on 26 Sept 2025, effective 1 Jan 2026. Consumers have been able to submit a single deletion request covering every registered broker via DROP since the portal opened on 1 Jan 2026, and registered data brokers have been required to access DROP at least once every 45 days and process pending deletion requests since 1 Aug 2026.
claims.note: Corrected on verification; catalogue text updated.

claims.claim: Clearview AI was fined under GDPR by France's CNIL (€20M, Oct 2022), Italy's Garante (€20M, Feb 2022), Greece's Hellenic DPA (€20M, July 2022) and the Netherlands' AP (€30.5M, Sept 2024). The UK ICO's £7.5M 2022 fine and enforcement notice were overturned by the First-tier Tribunal on jurisdictional (territorial/material-scope) grounds in Oct 2023; the Upper Tribunal reversed that ruling on 8 Oct 2025, holding UK data-protection law did apply because Clearview's processing related to monitoring UK residents' behaviour, and remitted the case to the First-tier Tribunal to decide the substantive appeal; Clearview was granted permission on 19 Dec 2025 to appeal the Upper Tribunal's decision to the Court of Appeal. Separately, Meta paused its plan to train AI on EU users' public Facebook/Instagram posts in June 2024 after Irish DPC pressure; following a Dec 2024 EDPB Opinion, Meta resumed EU AI training from 27 May 2025 with a required, in-app opt-out/objection mechanism for public posts.
claims.note: Corrected on verification; catalogue text updated.

claims.claim: Thomson Reuters v. Ross Intelligence (D. Del., Feb 11 2025): Judge Bibas ruled Ross's use of Westlaw headnotes to train a competing legal AI was not fair use; on Sept 29 2026 the Third Circuit affirmed in the first federal appellate ruling on AI-training fair use, while a footnote says its reasoning does not resolve the generative-AI training cases. Kadrey v. Meta (N.D. Cal., June 25 2025): Judge Chhabria granted Meta summary judgment that training Llama on the plaintiffs' books was fair use on that record, but warned a market-dilution theory could succeed for other plaintiffs. Bartz v. Anthropic (N.D. Cal.): the court held training on lawfully acquired books was fair use but acquiring copies via piracy was not; Anthropic agreed to a ~$1.5B settlement announced Sept 25 2025 (preliminary approval same day), and the court granted final approval on July 20 2026. NYT and other publishers v. OpenAI/Microsoft (S.D.N.Y., filed Dec 27 2023) remains pending: competing summary-judgment motions were filed Sept 4 2026 before Judge Sidney Stein, and a July 2026 sanctions motion over alleged evidence destruction/concealment is still undecided as of Oct 2026.
claims.note: Corrected on verification; catalogue text updated.

claims.claim: EU AI Act GPAI obligations (Arts. 51-56) became applicable on 2 Aug 2025, including the duty for general-purpose AI model providers to publish a 'sufficiently detailed summary' of training content using the EU AI Office's official template (published 24 July 2025); providers of GPAI models already on the market before 2 Aug 2025 have until 2 Aug 2027 to come into compliance.

Cloudflare launched its ‘pay per crawl’ feature in private beta on July 1, 2025, letting site owners charge AI crawlers per request and, by default, blocking unidentified AI crawlers unless paid or allowed; major AI crawlers publish distinct, documented user-agent tokens — OpenAI's GPTBot, Anthropic's ClaudeBot, Common Crawl's CCBot and Google's Google-Extended — with published purpose/contact info, and OpenAI and Common Crawl additionally publish their crawler IP ranges so site operators can identify and manage the traffic.

Reddit struck a real-time content-licensing deal with Google reported at roughly $60M/year (announced Feb 22, 2024; Reddit reportedly considered not renewing it as of July 2026). News Corp signed a 5-year global licensing deal with OpenAI on May 22, 2024, reported by WSJ to be worth over $250M. Axel Springer signed its OpenAI partnership on Dec 13, 2023. AP signed a 2-year archive-licensing deal with OpenAI on July 13, 2023. Shutterstock expanded its OpenAI partnership into a six-year data-licensing agreement on July 11, 2023, and reported $104M of AI-licensing revenue in 2023. Getty Images v. Stability AI: in the UK, the High Court (EWHC) ruled on Nov 4, 2025 that Getty had abandoned its primary training-copyright claim (for want of UK jurisdiction, since training occurred abroad) and found only limited trademark infringement from historic watermark reproduction, not copyright infringement; in the US, the original Delaware case was dismissed and Getty refiled in the Northern District of California (3:25-cv-06891), where a motion-to-dismiss ruling in April 2026 let most claims proceed and the case remains active.
claims.note: Corrected on verification; catalogue text updated.

claims.claim: A Stanford Internet Observatory report by David Thiel, published Dec 19/20, 2023, found roughly 1,008 suspected CSAM-linked URLs in LAION-5B's ~5.85B image-text pairs; LAION took the dataset down immediately and, working with the Internet Watch Foundation (IWF) and the Canadian Centre for Child Protection (C3P) — not NCMEC — matched against ~16.2M hash entries, finding an upper-bound 2,236 suspect links (subsuming Stanford's 1,008). LAION released the cleaned replacement, Re-LAION-5B (~5.5B pairs, in ‘research’ and ‘research-safe’ variants), on Aug 30, 2024.
claims.note: Corrected on verification; catalogue text updated.

claims.claim: On Jan 29, 2025, OpenAI and Microsoft said they were investigating whether a group linked to DeepSeek had improperly used OpenAI's API to distill its models, after Trump's AI czar David Sacks said there was ‘substantial evidence’ of distillation; OpenAI said it had banned suspect accounts. No lawsuit has been filed over this; it remains an unresolved allegation, not litigation. OpenAI reiterated the allegation to a US House committee in a Feb 12, 2026 update, saying its review ‘indicates that DeepSeek has continued to pursue activities consistent with adversarial distillation targeting OpenAI and other US frontier labs.’
claims.note: Corrected on verification; catalogue text updated.

claims.claim: A TIME investigation (Jan 2023) found OpenAI's outsourcing partner Sama paid Kenyan data-labelling workers about $1.32–$2 per hour in 2021–22 for safety-labelling work. The catalogue's higher figures (specialist review at ~$50+/hour, expert data at ~$30–200+/hour) are estimates from platform-reported ranges, not audited wage data.

Meta announced on June 12, 2025 a $14.3 billion investment in Scale AI for a 49% stake, valuing the company at just over $29 billion; as part of the deal, Scale AI founder/CEO Alexandr Wang left to lead a new ‘superintelligence’ team at Meta while Scale continued to operate independently under an interim CEO.

Clearview AI has been fined under GDPR by Italy's Garante (€20M, Feb 2022), France's CNIL (€20M, Oct 2022), Greece's Hellenic DPA (€20M, July 2022) and the Netherlands' AP (€30.5M, Sept 2024). Australia's OAIC found on 14 Oct 2021 that Clearview breached the Privacy Act 1988 and ordered it to stop collecting Australians' facial images and delete existing data; Clearview challenged this in the Administrative Appeals Tribunal but withdrew its appeal in August 2023 after the AAT found breaches, so the original 2021 determination and its cease-and-delete orders still stand as of the OAIC's August 2024 statement.

BuzzFeed News (Craig Silverman) reported on 9 Mar 2020 that Sensor Tower had owned at least 20 Android/iOS VPN and ad-blocking apps (e.g. Free and Unlimited VPN, Luna VPN, Mobile Data, Adblock Focus) with over 35 million downloads combined, which installed root certificates and fed usage/analytics data back into Sensor Tower's app-intelligence products without disclosing the ownership link; Apple and Google subsequently removed some of the apps.

Two expert-network insider-trading episodes reshaped industry compliance practice. (1) The Primary Global Research (PGR) prosecutions, 2010-11: PGR consultant Winifred Jiau was convicted at trial in June 2011 (part of the broader investigation that also implicated Galleon's Raj Rajaratnam) for tipping hedge funds via expert-network consultations; several other PGR-linked consultants and employees were separately charged. (2) The SEC/DOJ case against Mathew Martoma, a former SAC Capital (CR Intrinsic) portfolio manager, and Dr. Sidney Gilman: Gilman, a University of Michigan neurologist and a paid consultant on Gerson Lehrman Group's (GLG) scientific advisory board since 2002, was placed by GLG into dozens of paid 'expert network' consultations with Martoma from 2006; in July 2008 he gave Martoma early access to unfavorable Phase II trial results for the Alzheimer's drug bapineuzumab (Elan/Wyeth) before their public announcement, letting SAC-affiliated funds avoid losses/lock in profits of roughly $276M, the largest insider-trading haul ever charged at the time. The SEC sued Martoma, Gilman and CR Intrinsic in Nov 2012; Gilman settled with the SEC (disgorging ~$234,000) and testified as the government's cooperating witness; Martoma was convicted of securities fraud in federal court in Manhattan in Feb 2014.
